↕↔ Your choice — place a domino either way
💥 Bust! No legal pairing — turn lost.
A jump-and-capture game. Hop one of your stones over an adjacent enemy stone into the empty cell beyond, removing the stone you jumped. The first player who cannot jump loses.
A pile of stones. On your turn remove a perfect-square number of them — 1, 4, 9, 16, and so on. Take the last stone to win.
A queen sits on a grid and only ever moves toward the corner: any distance left, down, or diagonally down-left. The player who moves it onto the corner square wins.
A single strip, and BOTH players place the same mark (X). Whoever completes three X’s in a row wins — even using marks the other player placed.
After the first move, place TWO stones every turn. The first player to make six (or more) of their colour in an unbroken row, column, or diagonal wins.
Both players may place either an X or an O. "Order" wins by making five-in-a-row of a single symbol; "Chaos" wins if the board fills with no such line.
Both players place X or O. Order wants five-in-a-row; Chaos wants to stop it.
Claim a line; complete a box to claim it and go again. Most boxes wins.
Clear stones from the heaps. Take the last one to win — or flip on misère, where the last stone is the one to avoid.
Colour any empty cell in your colour — but never one orthogonally next to a cell you have already coloured (keep your patches apart). The first player who cannot colour a cell loses.
Colour the lines of a hexagon. Make a triangle in YOUR colour and you lose — someone always must.
Colour the map — but never next to the enemy. Spread wide, fence them in.
Colour the map — but no two of your own patches may touch. Run out of room and you lose.
Connect all three sides of the triangle with one connected group. Like Hex, it can never be a draw.
Connect all three sides with one group
Connect Four on a tube — lines wrap around the edges.
Connect Four where discs can leave: pop your own bottom disc and watch the column fall.

Connect Four wrapped into a tube: the left and right edges are joined, so a row of four can run right off one side and continue on the other. First to line up four of your colour — across (even around the seam), down, or diagonally — wins.
Connect your two sides with one unbroken chain of stones. It can never be a draw.
Dominoes for two — but BOTH of you can place either way. Last to fit one wins.
Doubles pay double and snake eyes pay 25. Greed, rewarded. Mostly.
Drop discs, line up four. Or seven. With up to six players.
Drop four, then slide — line them up or square them off.

Each turn, move one of your pawns one square straight forward into an empty cell, or one square diagonally forward to capture an enemy pawn sitting there. You win the instant one of your pawns reaches the far row, or if you capture all of the opponent’s pawns. There are no draws — someone always breaks through.
Eat a cookie + everything right & below. Don't eat the 💀!
Eat cookies (and everything right & below). Whoever eats the poison loses.

Emanuel Lasker’s twist on the mill game, played with ten men. Each turn you may EITHER place a man from your hand on an empty point OR slide a man already on the board to a neighbouring empty point — you no longer have to finish placing before you start moving. Line up three of your men on a marked line — a "mill" — to remove one enemy man (one not itself in a mill, if you can). Reduce your opponent to two men, or leave them with no move, to win.
Everyone plays the same mark (X). Completing any three-in-a-row LOSES — so force your opponent to make the line they’re trying to avoid.
Everyone plays X. Make three-in-a-row and you LOSE.

First, take turns dropping your four pieces onto any empty cells. Then take turns sliding one piece into an adjacent empty cell. Win the moment your four pieces form a straight line of four — or the corners of a 2×2 square.

First, take turns placing your nine men on the points. Then slide a man along a line to a neighbouring empty point. Any time you line up three of your men on a marked line — a "mill" — remove one enemy man (one that is not itself in a mill, if you can). Reduce your opponent to two men, or leave them with no move, to win.
Five stones in a row on a big board. Simple to learn, deep to master.
Flank a line of enemy discs to flip them. Most discs when the board fills wins.
Four tigers hunt twenty goats — trap the tigers or eat five goats.
Four-in-a-row wins — but three-in-a-row LOSES. Watch your step.
Four-in-a-row WINS, but three-in-a-row LOSES — and both are live at once. Build toward four while carefully avoiding an accidental three.
Get five-in-a-row — or capture five enemy pairs. Bracket a pair to snap it off the board.

Goats move first. While goats remain in hand, place one goat on any empty point; once all are placed, step a goat one point along a line to an empty neighbour. Tigers step along a line too, or jump an adjacent goat — landing just beyond — to capture it. Tigers win by eating enough goats; goats win by blocking every tiger so none can move.

Goats move first. While goats remain in hand, the goat player places one goat on any empty point. Once all goats are placed, a goat steps one point along a line to an empty neighbour. Tigers step along a line too, or jump an adjacent goat — landing on the empty point just beyond — to capture it. Tigers win by eating enough goats; goats win by blocking every tiger so none can move.
Hawaiian leap-and-capture. Jump over an enemy stone into the gap beyond. Last to jump wins.
Hop a stone onto an adjacent enemy to clobber it. Last to move wins.
Knights on a burning board: leap, scorch the square you left, outlast your rival.

Like Connect Four, but on your turn you may instead POP one of your own discs out of the bottom of a column — the whole stack above it drops one slot. First to line up four of your colour wins; beware, a pop can even complete your opponent’s line. A completely full board with no line is a draw — pop a disc to keep the game alive.
March pawns across the board. Capture diagonally. Reach the far row to win.
Mill! Tap an enemy piece to remove
Move a pawn one square straight forward into an empty cell, or one square diagonally forward to capture an enemy. Reach the far row, or capture every enemy pawn, to win. No draws.
Move an amazon like a queen, then shoot an arrow to burn a square. Trap your foe with no moves left.
Move and leave a wall behind. Box in your opponent — last to move wins.
Move one of your amazons like a chess queen (any distance in a straight line), then from its new square shoot an arrow the same way. The arrow burns its square forever. Trap your opponent to win.
Move your token one step to an open neighbour. The cell you leave becomes a permanent wall. Box your opponent in — the last player able to move wins. (Like light-cycles.)
One strip, and you BOTH play X. Whoever completes three X’s in a row wins.
Pair the dice, push your luck up the mountain — bust and you slide back.
Pass-and-play or take on the AI. Crank the knobs and make it weird.
Phase one: take turns placing your pieces. Once everyone has placed all their pieces, phase two begins — slide one of your pieces into an empty neighbouring cell each turn. Make a line to win.
Pick a pairing to advance your climbers.
Pick up all the seeds from one of your pits and sow them one-by-one into following pits. Land your last seed just right to capture. The most seeds in your store wins.

Pig with two dice and a wilder scoring twist. Roll both dice to add their total; roll any DOUBLE and it scores double — except double 1s, which pay a flat 25. A single 1 still busts the turn (but your bank is safe). Bank your points, and first to the target wins.

Pig with two dice. On your turn keep rolling both dice to add their total to your running turn score, then bank it. But roll a single 1 and you lose the whole turn’s points; roll two 1s (snake eyes) and you also lose your entire banked score. First to the target wins.
Place a disc so it flanks a straight line of enemy discs between your new disc and another of yours — all flanked discs flip to your colour. Most discs when the board fills wins.
Place a stone on any empty point. A group of stones with no empty neighbours (no "liberties") is captured. The first player to capture any enemy stone wins.
Place dominoes — you go vertical, the foe goes horizontal. Last to fit one in wins.
Place nine men, then slide them along the lines. Make a mill of three to snatch an enemy man. Grind them down to two.
Place one stone on any empty hexagon each turn. Red wins by linking the top and bottom edges with a connected chain; Gold links left and right. Hex can never be a draw.

Place one stone per turn. Win by lining up five of your colour, OR by capturing enough enemy pairs. Bracket exactly two enemy stones between two of yours (your-stone, enemy, enemy, your-stone) and that pair is snapped off the board.
Place stones and surround an enemy group to capture it. First capture wins!
Place TWO stones per turn; first to six-in-a-row wins.
Place your pieces, then slide them. Line them up to win.
Play exactly like Reversi — flank enemy discs to flip them — but the goal is reversed: when the board fills or nobody can move, the player with the FEWEST discs wins. Try to give discs away.

Players take turns placing one stone on any empty cell of the triangular board. You win by connecting all THREE sides of the triangle with a single connected group of your stones — the three corners each count for both of their sides. Stones are never moved or captured, and someone always connects, so Y can never be a draw.

Players take turns placing one stone on any empty hexagon. Red wins by linking the top edge to the bottom edge with a connected chain of red stones; Gold wins by linking the left edge to the right edge. Stones are never moved or captured, and exactly one player always completes a connection — Hex can never be a draw. With the pie rule on, the second player may answer the opening stone with a single Swap — claiming that stone as their own — instead of placing, which blunts the first-move advantage.
Pop the bottom disc from column {n}
Reduce the larger number ({hi}) toward zero
Remove a square number of stones — 1, 4, 9, 16… Take the last stone to win.
Reversi upside-down: flip everything at the ENEMY — fewest discs wins.
Roll again to climb higher, or stop to bank. Claim {toWin} columns to win.

Roll four dice and split them into two column sums; move your climbers up those columns (at most three columns per turn). Keep rolling to climb higher — but a roll with no legal pairing busts and wipes this turn’s progress. Stop to bank your climbers; reach the top of a column to claim it. First to claim the target number of columns wins.
Roll the die to build up a running total, then choose to bank it — but roll a 1 and you lose the whole turn’s points. First to reach the target score wins. Press your luck!
Roll to build points — but a 1 wipes your turn. Bank before you bust!

Scoop up all the seeds from one of your pits and drop them one-by-one into the pits going round. If your last seed lands in an opponent pit and makes it hold exactly 2 or 3, you capture those seeds — and keep grabbing backward while the pits before it also hold 2 or 3. First to more than half the seeds wins.
Six dots, fifteen connecting lines. Take turns colouring a line your colour. Completing a triangle of three dots all in your own colour LOSES — and someone always must.
Slide one of your pieces into the single empty point on the eight-pointed star. A piece may only move to the centre if it sits next to an enemy. Trap your opponent so they cannot move.
Slide the queen up, left, or diagonally toward the corner. Land on it to win.
Slide your pieces around the star. Block your opponent so they can’t move.
Sow seeds around the board and capture the pits you bring to 2 or 3.
Sow seeds, capture, and fill your store. Kalah rules.

Stones sit in one or more heaps. On your turn take stones from a single heap — up to the max-take limit, or as many as you like when it is set to “any”. In normal play the player who takes the very last stone wins; with the misère knob on, taking the last stone LOSES. (There’s a hidden winning strategy — can you find it?)
Swipe to merge tiles. Reach 2048 — or watch the AI try.
Swipe to slide all tiles one way; equal tiles that bump merge into one of double the value. A new tile appears after each move. Make a 2048 tile to win — but don’t fill the board.
Take turns colouring any empty cell — but you may never colour a cell orthogonally touching an ENEMY-coloured cell. Your own cells are fine to touch. The first player with no legal cell loses.
Take turns drawing one edge between two dots. Complete the fourth side of a 1×1 box to claim it and immediately take another turn. Most boxes when the grid is full wins.
Take turns dropping a disc into a column; it falls to the lowest empty slot. First to line up four of your colour in a row — across, down, or diagonally — wins.
Take turns marking an empty square. First to get your mark three-in-a-row (across, down, or diagonally) wins. With the knobs you can grow the board and the line length.
Take turns placing a domino on any two free side-by-side cells — vertical or horizontal, your choice (unlike Domineering, both players may use both). The first player who cannot fit a domino loses.
Take turns placing a stone on any empty point. The first player to get exactly five of their colour in an unbroken row — across, down, or diagonally — wins.

Take turns placing one stone on any empty cell of the triangular board. Win by joining all THREE sides of the triangle with a single connected group of your stones — the three corners each count for both of their sides. Like Hex, Y can never be a draw.
Take turns placing your stones. You win the moment four of your stones form the corners of a square — any size, and even tilted on a diagonal.
Tap a piece to pick it up
Tap an empty point to place
Tap an empty point to place a goat
Tap an empty square to slide
Tap stones from the right to take
Tap to place, or a piece to move
Tap where to shoot the arrow
The anti-Go: place stones, but never capture or self-trap. Run out of safe moves and you lose.
The board starts as a full checkerboard of two colours. On your turn, move one of your pieces onto an orthogonally-adjacent enemy piece, removing it. If you cannot move, you lose.
The chess champion's morris: ten men, and you may slide before you finish placing.
The grid is a chocolate bar; the top-left square is poisoned. On your turn eat a square and everything below-and-right of it. Whoever is forced to eat the poison loses.
The opposite of capture-Go: place a stone, but you may NEVER capture an enemy group or leave your own group without a liberty. The first player with no safe move loses.

Trails with a twist: your token moves like a chess knight — an L-shaped leap of two-then-one. The square you leap from becomes a permanent wall. Box your opponent in — the last player able to make a knight-leap wins.
Two dice, double the pace — but snake eyes eat your whole score.
Two numbers. On your turn, subtract any positive multiple of the smaller from the larger (the result must stay ≥ 0). The player who makes one of the numbers zero wins.
Two numbers. Subtract a multiple of the smaller from the larger. Make a zero to win.
Win when four of your marks form a square — any size, even tilted.
You and your opponent place dominoes on the grid, but you place yours vertically and they place theirs horizontally. The first player who cannot fit a domino loses.
You are the Fox, starting at the bottom. Reach the top row — the Hounds' home edge — to win. The Hounds only move forward (down) and win by boxing you in so you can't move.

You are the lone Fox and move one square diagonally in any direction; a wall of Hounds moves one square diagonally forward only. The Fox wins by slipping past to the far row; the Hounds win by trapping it.
